title: Parcel booking v2, design review
subtitle: What in this design will make it fail or hard to change, and what to decide before approving it.

verdict.text: Not as it is: the Book call waits on a 400–800 ms carrier quote against a 500 ms p95 goal, an accepted ADR contradicts how Tracking gets its data, and two promises customers rely on (no double charge, one owner of shipment status) have no mechanism. Decide first how booking gets the live quote, whether ADR-0002's central Data Service stays, and supersede ADR-0003; most other findings follow from those three.

stats.label: Promises without a mechanism
stats.note: no double charge, event order, rollback

stats.label: Contradictions
stats.note: ADR-0003, ADR-0002 vs ADR-0001, live quote vs 500 ms

facts.scope: Parcel booking v2 at Acme Logistics, design documents at commit 7c061c4 (no code exists yet)

decisions.title: How booking meets 500 ms at p95
decisions.chosen: Recommended: live quote before Book, held under a quote id
decisions.because: the carrier quote alone is 400–800 ms

decisions.title: Where services keep their data
decisions.chosen: Recommended: supersede ADR-0002, one schema per service, data team reviews migrations
decisions.because: the central Data Service makes every data change wait for a fifth team and is on every request

decisions.title: How Tracking learns of bookings and scans
decisions.because: polling the Booking service never sees a carrier scan

decisions.title: Owner of shipments.status
decisions.chosen: Recommended: Tracking owns the journey, Billing owns payment state
decisions.because: the payment notice arrives while the parcel travels and overwrites its status

decisions.title: Charge retries
decisions.chosen: Recommended: booking number as idempotency key, Billing owns retries
decisions.because: a retry after a timeout can charge again

decisions.title: Message broker
decisions.chosen: Not chosen; decide after consumers no longer rely on order
decisions.because: the three options differ on ordering

assumptions: The 400–800 ms carrier quote time is a typical range, so the p95 is at or above 800 ms.
The payment notice arrives within minutes of the charge, long before delivery.
Carrier scans identify a parcel by the carrier's tracking number from the label.
open: ADR-0004: which broker, retention for replay
Who answers customers about a charge outside office hours (proposal §16)
Whether the current payment provider accepts an idempotency key
How long the carriers honour a live quote

items.title: The Book call cannot meet 500 ms at p95: it waits on a 400–800 ms carrier quote
items.evidence:
The booking waits, in order: the Address Validator, up to 50 ms (`proposal.md:174`); the Pricing service (`:175`), which reads the contract discount through the Data Service (`:113`) and waits for the Carrier Gateway (`:176`), which waits for the carrier, 400–800 ms (`:126`). Then the booking is written through the Data Service (`:178`) and `ShipmentBooked` is published (`:179`). [high]

Stated times only: 50 + 400 = **450 ms** at the carrier's best, 50 + 800 = **850 ms** at its worst, before any of the network hops, the Data Service write and the publish. The goal is **500 ms at p95** (`quality-goals.md:8`), measured from request to confirmation (`:17`). A p95 sits at the slow end of the carrier's range, so the design misses the goal by up to 1.7× before counting a single hop. [high]

The goal at `proposal.md:27` puts the carrier's live quote in the confirmation, so with this flow the two goals cannot both hold. [high]
items.fix:
Take the carrier out of the Book call: ask for the live quote when the form is complete (a review step), hold it under a quote id with an expiry, and let `POST /bookings` reference the quote id. The Book call then waits on the Address Validator, one write and a publish. Call the Address Validator and Pricing in parallel rather than in turn. If that is not acceptable, agree a new number for Fast booking with its owner, Jelena Savkov.

**Safe when:** the carriers honour a quote for the expiry chosen (check the contracts, which this project may not change, `proposal.md:34`), the quote id is bound to the parcel's weight, zone and carrier, and the commercial team agrees what happens when a quote expires before Book.

items.title: `shipments.status` has two writers, and the payment notice overwrites where the parcel is
items.evidence:
§8 lists two writers for one field: `shipments.status` | Tracking service, Billing service (`proposal.md:215`). Tracking sets in transit and delivered from scans (`:186`); Billing sets invoiced (`:195`) and paid (`:196`). [high]

The card is charged right after the confirmation (`:192`), so the payment notice arrives while the parcel is still travelling, possibly before Tracking has created the shipment from `ShipmentBooked` [med]. The sequence is then paid → in transit (next scan) → delivered → invoiced: the field ends at invoiced for a parcel that was paid, and meanwhile the tracking page (`:188`) showed paid instead of where the parcel is. [high]

The Data Service API is `PATCH /tables/{table}` for every service (`:249`), so nothing enforces the owners in §8 either. [high]
items.fix:
Split the field: Tracking owns the journey (booked, in transit, delivered); Billing owns the payment state (charged, invoiced, paid) in its own record. The tracking page reads the first, finance the second.

**Safe when:** decided before either team builds against the shared field, and the store only lets the one owner write each field.

items.title: "Never charged twice" has no mechanism, and the retries make a second charge likely
items.evidence:
"If the charge call times out after 2 seconds, the Booking service retries the charge, up to three times" (`proposal.md:198`), then "A customer is never charged twice for one booking" (`:200`; goal owned by Ivana Kerac, `quality-goals.md:12`). [high]

A timeout does not say whether the charge happened: Billing may have charged the card and answered late. Neither §7.3 nor `POST /charges` (`:247`) names an idempotency key, and Billing's own timeout towards the provider is not stated. With a provider answering in 3 s, one booking sends up to **4** charge requests, each of which may succeed. [high]

After the retries "the Billing service e-mails the customer a payment link" (`:199`), but it is Booking that decided the charge failed; if Billing was the slow part, the customer can pay the link on top. [high] The charge is also a call made after the confirmation (`:192`) with no durable record: if the Booking service stops in between, nobody charges and no link goes out. [med]
items.fix:
Use the booking number as the idempotency key on `POST /charges`. Billing records the charge under that key before calling the provider (unique on booking number), passes the same key to the provider, and on a repeat returns the stored result instead of charging again. Better: Billing starts the charge from `ShipmentBooked` and owns the retries and the payment-link decision, so Booking no longer calls Billing at all.

**Safe when:** the current payment provider (kept, `proposal.md:36`) accepts an idempotency key or a lookup by merchant reference. Check this before approving.

items.title: Accepted ADR-0003 has Tracking poll Booking; the proposal has it consume events, and polling never sees a scan
items.evidence:
ADR-0003 is **accepted** (`:3`): "The Tracking service polls the REST API of the Booking service every minute, at `GET /bookings/changes?since=`" (`:20`), with the benefit that it "does not depend on the event format or on a broker" (`:25`). [high]

The proposal, which names the ADRs as its decisions (`proposal.md:8`), has Tracking receive every status change from the broker (`:134`), create the shipment on `ShipmentBooked` (`:184`) and update status from `CarrierScan` (`:186`). Accepted ADR-0001 also has the services exchange events through a broker (`:20`). `GET /bookings/changes` is not in the interfaces table (§10). [high]

Polling the Booking service cannot meet ADR-0003's own context, "every status change of a shipment" (`:9`): scans go to the Carrier Gateway (`proposal.md:127`), never to Booking. Built as accepted, the tracking page never moves past booked and the 2-minute tracking goal (`quality-goals.md:13`) fails. [high]
items.fix:
Write a new ADR, "Tracking consumes events", superseding ADR-0003, and mark ADR-0003 superseded. Keep what ADR-0003 valued: decide how long events are kept so Tracking can replay after an outage (ADR-0004's open question, `:27`).

**Safe when:** both the tracking and booking teams build from the new ADR; the event rules in the events finding below are part of it.

items.title: ADR-0002's Data Service puts a fifth team into every release and onto every request
items.evidence:
v2 exists because "every release waits for all four" teams (`proposal.md:14`), and ADR-0001 promises "Each team releases its service on its own schedule" (`:24`). ADR-0002 puts every table except tariffs behind one Data Service run by the data team (`:17-19`): "A new table, a new column or a new query is a request in the data team's backlog, released with the Data Service every two weeks" (`proposal.md:147`). Any feature that stores something new waits for a fifth team's release. [high]

"The Data Service is on the path of every request that reads or writes data" (`ADR-0002:25`): five services call it (`proposal.md:89-93`), the Book call twice, and it has no availability target. [high]

Its API is `GET` and `PATCH /tables/{table}` (`proposal.md:249`): services still depend on tables and columns, the problem ADR-0002 set out to fix (`:11`). Two calls share no transaction, so Billing's invoice and status writes (`proposal.md:194-195`) and Booking's write and publish (`:178-179`) can half-happen, and an outbox is impossible because no service has a store of its own. [high]
items.fix:
Supersede ADR-0002: each service owns its tables in its own schema (they can share one database server) and reads no other service's schema; data crosses by API or event. Keep ADR-0002's real aim, every schema change reviewed, by making the data team a required reviewer of every migration.

If ADR-0002 stays, the design must add transactions or an outbox inside the Data Service, per-table write permissions matching §8, an availability target, and ADR-0001's "own schedule" must be reworded.

**Safe when:** decided now. Nothing is built, so nothing has to move; after January 2027 every service is written against the Data Service API.

items.title: Events: order is expected from a broker not yet chosen, and duplicates and lost publishes are not handled
items.evidence:
"The Tracking service relies on the message broker to deliver the events of one shipment in the order they were published" (`proposal.md:232`), while "Which broker product we run is to be decided later" (`:234`; ADR-0004 `:21`). The three options differ on exactly this [med]. Publish order would not be enough anyway: the Gateway publishes in the order callbacks arrive, not the order the carrier scanned [med].

Nothing says what a consumer does with a duplicate. Billing issues the invoice when `ShipmentDelivered` arrives (`:194`); a redelivered event or a second delivered scan gives a second invoice. [high]

The booking is written (`:178`), then `ShipmentBooked` is published (`:179`), as two steps. If the publish fails, the booking stays confirmed but Tracking never creates the shipment: no `ShipmentDelivered`, so no invoice. [high]
items.fix:
Make consumers independent of order and duplicates so that any broker works. Every event gets an id. Tracking applies a scan only if its time (already in every event, `:231`) is later than the shipment's current status, and delivered never goes back. Billing issues at most one invoice per shipment (a unique key). Publish through an outbox written in the same transaction as the booking, which depends on the ADR-0002 decision.

**Safe when:** the event time is the carrier's scan time, not the time the Gateway received the callback.

items.title: No timeout or fallback for the carriers or the payment provider
items.evidence:
The only timeouts in the documents are the Address Validator's 50 ms (`:153`) and the charge call's 2 s (`:198`). Booking → Pricing → Carrier Gateway → carrier are three nested waits (`:175-177`) with no timeout at any hop, and nothing says what the customer sees when a carrier does not answer. Billing → Payment provider (`:139`) has none either. [high]

Scans arrive as callbacks (`:127`). Nothing says whether a carrier retries when the Gateway is down, or how a missed scan is noticed. A lost delivered scan means no `ShipmentDelivered`, so no invoice (`:194`). [high]

The Address Validator shows the design knows how: a budget, a fallback and a flag for a person (`:153-155`). [high]
items.fix:
For each outside dependency write down the timeout, the retry and what the user sees. Timeouts shrink inwards (carrier < Gateway < Pricing < Booking) so no caller gives up before its callee. When a quote fails: offer another carrier, or confirm at the tariff estimate, which is a rule for the commercial team. For scans: get each carrier's callback retry policy, and add a check that asks the carrier's scan API about shipments with no scan for a set time.

**Safe when:** the commercial team agrees which price applies when the live quote fails.

items.title: No flow registers the parcel with the carrier or makes its label
items.evidence:
Booking (§7.1) asks the carrier for a quote only; no step tells the carrier the parcel exists. The Gateway "writes each label to `labels`" (`:129`) but no flow asks for one, and its only endpoint is `POST /quotes` (`:245`). Counter staff print labels (`:166`), yet whether label printing moves to the Gateway is an open question (`:291`). [high]

The label carries the carrier's tracking number (`:304`), which is what a carrier's scan refers to [med]; without it the Gateway cannot put the shipment number on a `CarrierScan` (`:231`). The first rollout step is three counters (`:270`).
items.fix:
Add the step: on `ShipmentBooked`, the Gateway registers the shipment with the carrier and stores the label, the carrier's tracking number and the mapping it needs for scans. Keep it out of the Book call, which already misses its goal. Add the label endpoint to §10 and decide where the counter prints.

**Safe when:** decided before the January counter step.

items.title: Availability and scale have no number, and no load is sized anywhere
items.evidence: "The platform must be highly available and scale for peak season" (`:9`) has no percentage and no load. Peak season has dates (`:24`) but no bookings per hour, and nothing estimates what web and mobile booking add to today's counter volume. Fast booking's p95 is taken "over all bookings of a day" (`:17`), which hides the peak hour. The Data Service and the broker are on every path and have no target. [high]
items.fix:
Per journey (book, tracking page, invoices): an availability number, the peak load it must hold (bookings per minute at the busiest hour), and p95 per hour rather than per day.

**Safe when:** the figures come from the counter app's own peak, which runs from mid-November (`:24`); this season can be measured now, before v2 goes live.

items.title: The broker is still undecided two months before go-live, and the teams have not run one
items.evidence: ADR-0004 is Proposed: "To be decided later, after the platform team has tried each option" (`:21`). All services go live in January 2027 (`proposal.md:270`), and "The teams have not run a message broker before" (`:285`). The "small interface of their own" (`:22`) hides the client API, not the delivery guarantees. Of its open questions, night on-call (`:26`) is already answered by §12, "the platform team covers nights and weekends" (`proposal.md:266`); retention for replay (`:27`) is needed once Tracking consumes events. [high]
items.fix:
Set a date for the decision that leaves time for a trial and runbooks before January, record the night on-call from §12 in the ADR, and decide retention. Once the event rules above are in place, the choice is about operations only.

**Safe when:** the trial covers a redelivery and a consumer restart, not only the happy path.

items.title: Going back to the counter app has no path for parcels already booked in v2
items.evidence: "Until June 2027 the counter app stays ready to take bookings again" (`:276`). From January, bookings at three counters live in v2's Data Service while the counter app keeps its own database (`:13`). Nothing says who tracks and invoices parcels booked in v2 if you switch back, or how finance sees both systems' invoices for those months. [high] While both systems book, the carriers' scan callbacks have to reach both [guess].
items.fix:
Write the rollback rule: switching back stops new bookings in v2 only; v2's Tracking and Billing keep running for parcels already booked there until they are delivered and invoiced. Say how finance reports across both systems from January to June.

**Safe when:** v2's Tracking and Billing can run with booking switched off.

items.title: Inbound callbacks from carriers and the payment provider are not authenticated
items.evidence: §11 covers customers, staff, service tokens and cards. Scan callbacks (`:127`) and payment notices (`:50`) come in from outside, and §11 says nothing about them. A forged delivered scan would issue an invoice (`:194`); a forged payment notice would mark a shipment paid (`:196`). [high]
items.fix:
Verify each callback as its sender allows (signature, shared secret or mutual TLS), and accept a scan only for a tracking number the Gateway issued.

**Safe when:** each carrier's and the provider's callback security has been checked; some may offer only an IP allow-list.

items.title: Cash at the counter is not designed, and the counters go first
items.evidence: "Do cash payments at the counter go through the Billing service as well?" is open (`:293`). The charge flow always charges a card (`:192`), and the first rollout step puts walk-in customers at three counters on v2 (`:270`). [high]
items.fix: Decide before January: either Billing records a cash payment, so there is still one invoice flow, or the first counter step serves card payers only.

items.title: Contract discounts have no named writer and sit in another team's table
items.evidence: Pricing reads the contract discount from `customers` (`:113`), which only Booking writes (`:213`). Nobody is named to enter contract terms; the commercial team sets tariffs only (`:44`). The read also adds a Data Service call to the Book call. [high]
items.fix: Keep contract discounts with the tariffs in the Pricing database, entered in the same admin page, so a quote reads nothing from `customers`. Check that no personal data comes with them (`:260`).

items.title: The tracking goal has no percentile and depends on an unstated carrier delay
items.evidence: "A carrier scan shows on the tracking page within 2 minutes" (`:13`), measured from the carrier's scan time (`:20`). It has no percentile, and the carriers' delay before they send a callback is not stated anywhere. [high]
items.fix: Add a percentile, and either measure from the moment the Gateway receives the callback or state each carrier's callback delay.

items.title: The interfaces table misses endpoints the design relies on
items.evidence: §10 has no `GET /bookings/changes` (ADR-0003 `:20`), no label endpoint, no scan callback, no payment notice endpoint and no tariff admin. [high]
items.fix: Add them once the tracking and label decisions are taken, with the callbacks' authentication.

sections.title: The design as written
sections.intro: Drawn from the proposal's §5 diagram and §6–§7 text. A label with "waits" is a synchronous call where the caller waits; the other links are events or callbacks. Flagged parts carry findings.

components.label: Counter staff
components.note: Book for walk-in customers and print labels.

components.label: Commercial team
components.note: Sets tariffs in the Pricing admin page.

components.label: Web app
components.note: Booking, tracking and invoices; counter role adds labels.

components.label: Booking service
components.note: Takes a booking, checks the address, gets the price, confirms, then charges.
details: The Book call waits on a 400–800 ms carrier quote against 500 ms p95; it retries charges with no idempotency key.

components.label: Address Validator
components.note: Register in memory, 50 ms budget with a fallback.
details: After 50 ms the address is accepted as typed and flagged for staff.

components.label: Pricing service
components.note: Tariff plus live carrier quote; tariff alone for the estimate.
details: Waits on the Gateway with no timeout; reads contract discounts from another team's table.

components.label: Carrier Gateway
components.note: Only part that talks to the carriers: quotes, labels, scans.
details: No timeout or fallback towards carriers; no flow creates labels; callbacks not authenticated.

components.label: Tracking service
components.note: Keeps shipment status, serves the tracking page.
details: Accepted ADR-0003 says it polls Booking; the proposal says events. Relies on broker ordering.

components.label: Billing service
components.note: Charges cards, issues invoices, follows payments.
details: Second writer of shipments.status; no duplicate handling for invoices or charges.

components.label: Data Service
components.note: Every table except tariffs, behind GET and PATCH /tables/{table}.
details: On every request, no availability target, no transactions; every data change waits for its two-week release.

components.label: Pricing database
components.note: Table tariffs, read through a 15-minute cache.

components.label: Message broker
details: Tracking relies on its ordering, which the options do not share.

components.label: Carrier APIs
components.note: Brzopak, Kolibri Kurir, Tranzit Plus. Quote 400–800 ms.

components.label: Payment provider
details: Not stated; idempotency support not checked.

components.label: Postal register
components.note: Streets and house numbers, loaded nightly.

steps.text: The client sends the booking; the clock for the 500 ms p95 goal starts.
Address check, waits up to 50 ms, then accepts the address as typed.
Waits for the final price.
Reads the contract discount from customers: another waiting hop.
Waits for the live quote, no timeout stated.
Carrier quote: 400–800 ms. With the address check, 450–850 ms before any hop.
Writes bookings.
Publishes ShipmentBooked, a separate step from the write: no outbox.
After the confirmation, charges the card; on a 2 s timeout retries up to three times, with no idempotency key.
ShipmentBooked arrives (ADR-0003 says polling instead).
Creates the shipment.
Scan callback, not authenticated, no retry policy stated.
Publishes CarrierScan; order relied on from a broker not chosen.
CarrierScan arrives.
Sets shipments.status: in transit or delivered.
Publishes ShipmentDelivered.
The tracking page reads the status.
Charge request after the confirmation.
Charges the card; Billing's timeout not stated.
Payment notice, likely while the parcel is in transit.
Sets shipments.status to paid: the second writer of that field.
ShipmentDelivered arrives; no duplicate handling.
Writes the invoice, then sets status to invoiced: two calls, no transaction.

Each booking for that carrier waits in Booking → Pricing → Gateway with no timeout at any hop and no stated message to the customer. Waiting requests hold capacity in three services, which slows bookings for the other two carriers as well [med]. If that carrier's scan callbacks stop too, its delivered parcels are not invoiced.
No timeout per hop, no fallback price, no peak load to size for.
The payment provider answers in 3 s for an hour
Booking times out at 2 s and retries up to three times: up to 4 charge requests per booking, each of which may succeed. Then Billing e-mails a payment link that the customer may also pay.
No idempotency key on `POST /charges` or towards the provider; Booking, not Billing, decides that the charge failed.
The Data Service is down for ten minutes, or its release goes wrong

Booking cannot write bookings, Pricing cannot read discounts, Tracking cannot store scans, Billing cannot invoice: every flow stops at once. Nothing says whether events consumed in that window are retried or lost.
The Data Service is on every path (ADR-0002:25), with no availability target and no way to degrade.

blocks.title: Before approval
items: **How the Book call meets its goal.** Live quote before Book, held under a quote id, or a new number for Fast booking. Owners: Jelena Savkov, with the commercial team on quote validity.
**Keep or supersede ADR-0002.** This decides whether outboxes and transactions are possible and whether ADR-0001's independent release holds, so it comes before any service is built.
**How Tracking learns of bookings and scans.** Supersede ADR-0003 with events, including how long events are kept for replay.
**One owner for `shipments.status`.** Split the journey (Tracking) from the payment state (Billing).
**Charge idempotency.** The booking number as the key, provider support confirmed, Billing owning retries and the payment link. Owner: Ivana Kerac.
**Event rules any broker satisfies.** Event id, ordering by event time, monotonic status, at most one invoice per shipment, outbox.

blocks.title: Then change the design
items: Availability and peak load numbers, measured on the counter app during the peak season that starts now.
The carrier registration and label step, and cash at the counter, before the January counter step.
A timeout, a retry and what the user sees, for every outside dependency.
Authentication for scan callbacks and payment notices.
The rollback rule for parcels already booked in v2.
Contract discounts moved to Pricing; a percentile on the tracking goal; §10 completed.

blocks.title: Can wait
items: **The broker product (ADR-0004)**, once consumers no longer depend on order, with a fixed date that leaves time for a trial before January.
**Who answers customers about a charge outside office hours** (`proposal.md:292`): a support question, not an architecture one.
**Services by team (ADR-0001).** Argued from four teams that block each other; the problem is the data decision around it, not the split.
**The Address Validator's 50 ms budget.** A timeout, a fallback and a flag for staff: the model the other dependencies should follow.
**The tariff cache with 15 minutes of staleness.** Accepted by its owner, with a reason (tariffs change weekly and take effect on Monday).
**The estimate from the tariff alone while the customer types.** It keeps the carrier out of the form.
**The Carrier Gateway as the only part that talks to carriers.** Keep it; it needs timeouts and the label step, not a different shape.
**Cards stay with the provider; Billing holds a token.**
**Path versioning for breaking changes.**
**The rollout in steps with four weeks without a severe incident between them.**

sections.title: What this review did not cover

items: **Code.** None exists yet (`README.md:4`); this reviews the seven documents only.
**Load and cost.** The documents give no peak figures and no cost, so nothing was sized or priced.
**The carriers' and the payment provider's own terms.** Idempotency keys, quote validity, callback retries and callback security are not in the repo and must be checked with them.
**Security beyond §11.** No threat model was done; the callback finding is what the documents themselves show.
**Operations in detail.** Deployment, observability, backups and cluster capacity are described in one paragraph (§12) and were not reviewed further.
**The Web and Mobile apps' own design** and the user experience.

blocks.title: Assumptions I made instead of asking
items: The 400–800 ms carrier time is a typical range, so the p95 is at or above 800 ms.
The payment notice arrives within minutes of the charge, long before delivery.
Carriers identify a scanned parcel by their own tracking number from the label.
